articles.text: Pied mont High School seniors, the Class of 2022, celebrated their graduation with a grand commencement ceremony on Thursday, June 2 at Witter Field. articles.text: Piedmont’s City Council directed the Park Commission to form a subcommittee to memorialize the Sidney Dearing family. At a May 16 meeting, the council discussed the possibility of the naming of the triangle park at the intersection of Magnolia and Wildwood Avenues as “Dearing Family Memorial Park,” in memorial of Sidney Dearing. Sidney and Irene Dearing were Piedmont’s first black homeowners. The couple purchased a home in the city in 1924 and were driven out by a mob of white Piedmont residents. The Piedmont Police Department did little to help the family as a 500-person mob demanded the family’s removal. Instead of taking action on the agenda item on May 16, City Administrator Sara Lillevand advised City Council to “slow down on the name itself, and provide more opportunity for public engagement on this important effort.” Lillevand explained that there have been numerous calls from residents asking the city to address the treatment of the Dearing family and to publicly acknowledge the behavior of past public officials. The triangle park being considered is located across the street from the former Dearing home. Several residents called in asking if City Council had discussed the proposal with residents in the area of Magnolia and Wildwood Avenue, as well as Dearing’s descendants. On Wednesday, June 1, Park Commissioners considered establishing a subcommittee to make recommendations on an appropriate way to memorialize the family. Lillevand introduced commissioners to Cornelia Sylvester, a Certified Professional Coach, who has been working with the city staff as a consultant since September 2020 facilitating antibias training and discussions. “We looked at the Dearing story not as a unique case, but as a case that is common in most suburbs across the United States. We wanted to think about what each person’s role was in getting this family out of Piedmont,” Sylvester said. “There were several governmental bodies that played a large part.” Sylvester presented questions for commissioners to consider: how many people and facets of the government did it take to accomplish the goal of removing the family? What was preserved by moving the Dearings out of town? What was lost? And at what critical junctures could this incident have been prevented? “In order to have homogenous communities, it takes a considerable amount of effort and exclusion,” she explained. Lillevand explained that city staff was “new” to the Sidney Dearing story in 2020, when Sylvester first began working with the city on bias training. City staff role played as members of the community in 1924, acting out the removal of the Dearing family. “It was powerful, impactful, and memorable,” Lillevand said. articles.text: St. Francis is known for that famous saying “preach the gospel, and if you have to, use words.” God is probably less concerned about what we believe and more concerned about the way we act. When we get right down to it, there are simply too many words flying around and not enough meaningful action. And as Christians approach Easter, the celebration of Jesus’ resurrection, it is easy for us to get sidetracked by words in the form of creeds, liturgies and theologies. These provide enough words to suffocate the real story that was all about meaningful action. It’s in that context that I share what I consider to be an Easter Story. A few years ago, Elizabeth Gilbert, author of “Eat, Pray, Love”, wrote about an incident that changed her life. She was riding the midtown bus in New York City in evening rush hour traffic. The weather was the worst January had to offer, complete with sleet and gusting wind. To quote her, “It sucked”. The bus was moving at a crawl, tempting her to get out and walk, but the cold icy world she was staring at through the window paralyzed her. The depression in that mobile metal tomb was palpable. One of San Francisco’s premier party bands for 25 years, this interactive 11-piece all-star group has gained a national reputation for their high energy performances, incredible musical variety, and “anything-can-happen” hi-jinx. David Martin is a Bay Area native who began his musical career at the age of six. Known for his powerful vocals and sparkling guitar work, David was a founding member of legendary San Francisco “New Wave” faces The Lloyds and The Buzztones. articles.text: The City of Piedmont is planning a program that offers free compost for Piedmont residents to pick up every Friday during the summer months, as weather and availability allow. This pilot program is different than recent free compost giveaway events, in that the compost will be available to residents to pick up from an unattended pile every Friday starting at 8:00 a.m. The compost will be available in a dumpster box located outside the entrance to the City’s Corporation Yard located at 898 Red Rock Road. The site is now open every Friday and will close for the season in the fall. The compost is firstcome, first-served, and City staff cannot guarantee availability of compost. To pick up compost, residents should bring a shovel, container, and gloves to load the materials. Pickup trucks must have a tarp on their loads. The compost originally comes from the green waste (yard trimmings and food waste) that is collected by Republic Services in communities participating in curbside organics collection services. The green waste is brought to a processing plant in Richmond where it is converted into a highly aerobic, microbial compost. The compost making process involves the careful mixing of the waste and monitoring of the carbon to nitrogen ratio, CO2, temperature, and moisture. As the compost is locally based and free, it models the concept of a circular economy, where a resource is used and reused in a cycle that turns “waste” back into new products or materials than can reenter the supply chain. This process helps to keep organic materials from emitting greenhouse gasses in the landfill and creates opportunities to use these nutrient-rich resources to regenerate our soils. Mixing compost with soil aids in water retention and pest control and helps plants thrive. Senate Bill 1383, a state law that went into effect January 1, 2022, requires all municipalities to collect organic waste from residents and businesses and that it be composted. articles.text: Cit y Financial Plan ner Michael Szczech facilitated a public hearing on the proposed fiscal year (FY) 2022-2023 budget at the most recent city council meeting on June 6. This was the first public hearing on the proposed budget, as well as a proposed levy of the municipal Services Special Tax. Piedmont’s Finance Department is budgeting $33,864,402 in General Fund expenditures, an increase of 7% from last year’s [FY 2021-22] projected expenditures. Property-related tax revenue decreases The report prepared by Szczech found that property-related taxes, the city’s primary revenue source, saw a decrease of $739,280 based on the city’s projection one year ago, over the 2021-22 projected actual. The proposed budget this year consists of property tax revenues budgeted at $16,875,000, a 5.5% increase. “The increase is [due to] a high volume of home sales at record high prices, which increased the assessed valuation of those homes at 120%,” explained Szczech. The Parcel Tax revenue, based on the measure approved by a majority of voters in March 2020, is estimated at $2,522,000, a 4% increase over the 2021-22 projection. “The housing market continues to be strong and is a key factor in maintaining the stability of City revenues,” Szczech said. “There is no assurance this trend will continue, as the overall economy faces serious headwinds with rising interest rates and inflation. Real Property Transfer Tax receipts have been higher than [budgeted] through the first nine months of the fiscal year and are trending to surpass the budget by approximately $2.2 million.” Recreation revenue Revenue generated by the city Recreation Department is now back at pre-pandemic levels, the report showed. The proposed budget accounts for an increase of $276,00 in revenue from the prior year. The new budget assumes that programs will no longer be impacted by COVID-19-related revenue loss. “Recreation program revenue has returned to a normal [pre-pandemic] state after being severely impacted by cancelled programs and reduced capacity in varying degrees between March 2020 and June 2021 due to COVID-19. Recreation staff did an outstanding job in navigating the fluctuating rules and guidelines issued by County and State Health officials,” said Szczech. Pre-school revenue is budgeted at a slightly smaller increase of $165,000 over 2021-22 projections. Programming was increased from 4-day to 5-day programs, but revenue suffered due to reduced class sizes. Preschool programs next year are at pre-pandemic, full class-size levels. Facility rentals for use at 801 Magnolia Avenue is budgeted at $45,000 for FY 2022-23. Construction market exceeds budget expectations FY 2020-2021 was a record year for construction and remodeling costs, increasing 28% over the prior year, and continues to remain high. Staff is projecting to exceed the annual budget this fiscal year by $200,000, or 17%. Administrative costs related to this market include building permits, planning fees, plan check fees, general plan maintenance fees, and records management fees. “This category continues to surprise us. Consistent with the City’s overall budget philosophy, staff is budgeting for declines in revenue in all areas of this category as staff does not expect the high level of activity to continue as the city faces mounting economic uncertainty,” said Szczech.

articles.text: Piedmont residents have a wealth of opportunities to volunteer within their community and the East Bay this summer. Thanks to suggestions from residents, Piedmont Post has compiled a list of organizations that are currently seeking volunteers. Wardrobe for Opportunity Oakland Wardrobe for Opportunity Oakland provides access to transformational career support services for low-income individuals seeking employment. The organization was founded in 1995 to help low-income women look professional in workplace settings and has since evolved to provide a complete suite of career development services to men, women, and youth. There are various ways you can volunteer with the organization, which is seeking volunteers to conduct mock interviewers, style clients, facilitate workshops, and process donations. Wardrobe for Opportunity also accepts gently-used and new clothing donations. Visit https://www.wardrobe.org/donate to learn more. e-Buddies E-Buddies promotes social inclusion online for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities such as autism and Down syndrome. Like a modern version of a letter writing program, the organization pairs your child and a child with developmental disabilities as e-mail pen pals. It is a great opportunity for students who would like to volunteer remotely and helps encourage technology literacy and communication skills. Participants are matched based on age, gender, and similar interests; anyone over the age of 10 and with parents’ permission can participate in e-Buddies. To sign up, visit https://www.bestbuddies. org/what-we-do/ebuddies/. Lake Merritt Institute Lake Merritt Institute partners with local citizens and Oakland Unified School District students to help keep Lake Merritt’s shoreline and creeks clean on a weekly basis. Volunteers meet at the Institute office on the 2nd floor of the Boating Center, 568 Bellevue Avenue next to the parking lot, in Lakeside Park. The office entrance is up the stairs behind the Boathouse office at the end of the building. Volunteers usually work 2-3 hours during a shift. Gloves are provided. Individuals who have been trained may also work alone using one of the four “U-Clean-It” boxes around the Lake where you will find gloves, trash bags, barrels, nets, directions and a sign-in sheet. Visit https://lakemerrittinstitute.org/how-you-can-help/ to sign up. Mercy Brown Bag The Mercy Brown Bag program distributes over 1 million pounds of food every year, thanks to hundreds of volunteers. The effort was launched in 1982 by residents at the Mercy Retirement & Care Center who saw that seniors in their Oakland neighborhoods were experiencing food insecurity. There are many ways to volunteer, including distributing lunch bags to homebound seniors, helping at distribution sites, and translating written materials. Visit https:// mercybrownbag.org/volunteer/ to sign up. Is there a volunteer effort or organization that you would like to highlight? Interested in expanding this list? articles.text: Sometimes when we think about bringing creativity into our family life, it can feel overwhelming. There are so many competing needs and objectives in our busy lives, how can we possibly make room for one more thing? As I reflect on this question, I am thinking about a science experiment that I did with my son when he was about 5 years old. We took a mason jar and filled it with rocks and asked the question, “Is it full?” To which, he dutifully answered, “Yes!” And then we poured smaller rocks in and around the larger rocks. Again, we asked, “Is it full?” This time he answered “Yes” with a little more hesitation. Then we poured sand in, which filled the space around the smaller and larger rocks. This time he knew it wasn’t full, even though the jar looked completely full. For the last step, we added water and filled it to the brim. The point is, there is always more room if we are willing to fill some of the cracks and crevices. The key is how do we fill those things in a way that feels easy and meaningful, but without exhausting ourselves even more? If you are looking to bring more creativity into your family, maybe it’s not about big projects with epic outcomes. Maybe it’s about tiny micro-moments that are tucked in between soccer camp and family vacations. Here are just a few ideas for fitting creativity into the summer space that already exists, but maybe we aren’t paying attention to it: • Airplane Coloring Challenge Doing some traveling this summer? articles.text: Children’s Fairyland is bringing back its annual Book Festival after a two-year pandemic-driven pause. The festival, now in its fifth year, will feature 25 Bay Area children’s authors and illustrators for a full day of story-time. A mix of well-established and emerging authors will be present. Six authors and illustrators will give 25-minute book presentations and live art demonstrations at Fairyland’s Emerald City Stage. Headliners include award-winning authors Mac Barnett, JaNay Brown-Wood, Johanna Ho, C.V Monterrubio, Wednesday Kirwan and Nina LaCour. Attendees will have a chance to purchase books which can be signed by featured authors during scheduled meet-and-greet times, which will be broken up into five-minute time slots. Student writers age 8 through 12 from Fairyland’s Youth Writer’s Workshop will then share a joint reading at the Youth Author Table in the afternoon. Other featured authors and illustrators this year are John Casselberry, Madeline Connor, Angela Dalton, Cindy Derby (2021 Caldecott Honor for Outside In), Hayley Diep, Meg Fleming, Alia Gabres, Michael Genhart (2022 Pura Belpre Award for May Your Life Be Deliciosa), Jill Guerra, Felicia Hoshino, Illustoria, Nancy Johnson James, Dawood Marion, Constance Moore, Christina Newhard, Jane Park (2015-2016 Asian Pacific American Librarians Association’s Asian Pacific American Award for Juna’s Jar), Keely Parrack, Lea Redmond, Nadia Salomon, Victoria Sanchez, Simone Shin, Emma Bland Smith, Meera Sriram (2021 South Asia Book Award for A Gift for Amma), Meredith Steiner, and Justine Villanueva. Also participating is Maggie Tokuda Hall, a Piedmont High School graduate whose work of fiction for young adults. Squad, won the Poppy Award in 2021. Festival attendance is free with park admission. The festival takes place on Saturday, June 1, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Learn more at www.fairyland. org or visit the park at 699 Bellevue Avenue in Oakland.

articles.text: Good evening, everyone. I’d first like to begin by thanking all of you, parents, students, teachers, and administrators, for fostering my growth both intellectually and as an individual throughout my four years in high school. So, Piedmont High School class of 2022, we finally get a break. We’re finally done thinking about anything intellectual for the next couple of weeks. Oh wait, nope! You have to listen to one of Jacob’s speeches, which you best bet will have some sort of intellectual reference. Now I promise you that I’ll only make one such reference this time, and that’s going to be “Frankenstein” by Mary Shelley, so for those of you that haven’t read it, you have about 30 seconds to scour SparkNotes before I start making my references. Don’t worry, I know many of you all have experience doing this. But really, I am genuinely honored to speak in front of you today, to represent the successes of this amazing class. It’s safe to say that our class has been through a lot together. We’ve endured a year and a half of distance learning during what many would consider the heart of our high school experience. We’ve gone through the horror of processing mass shootings, both school and racially motivated shootings, that have really become too many to count. We’ve experienced first-hand a worsening political climate. Every day, we expect to wake up to some shocking headline about the future of our country or our planet. The examples go on. Oh, yeah, and I almost forgot. About a week ago today our senior prank was…well, let’s not talk about that. But it is because of these difficult times we’ve shared together that we’ve become more united. We can collectively bond over many of these struggles, which drives us to create change in response to those struggles. And change we’ve seen. Everywhere you look, you’re bound to see an activist of some sort, whether someone who directly helped the community demonstrate a commitment to social justice, or simply someone who you can have insightful, introspective conversations with, conversations that are the basis for change. I feel as if I could go up to any one of you right now and have one of these insightful conversations. That is the unique unity and passion of our class at work. You see, society is like Dr. Frankenstein: a flawed society creates flawed but passionate individuals, and we are those passionate individuals. Frankenstein’s creature was powerful, and much of that power may be attributed to his flaws, but also his drive to come to terms with Dr. Frankenstein. He was distanced by society solely due to his appearance, as I’m sure many of you may feel detached from a society controlled by older generations that hold different values. But let’s not let the flaws of society destroy us and fall to the same fate as Frankenstein’s creature. Let’s use our drive and persistence; let’s come to terms with our Dr. Frankenstein. Let’s carry forward in our lives with this unity and passion that we’ve developed here at Piedmont High School. Let’s not be that apathetic, meme-obsessed, social-media generation that those in Washington and Wall Street think we are. We aren’t new to creating change. We’ve done it before, and looking out at you guys right now, I’m optimistic that we can do it again. articles.text: JACK STEIN Cross Country & Track Jack Stein did what no other PHS athlete has done in nearly 20 years, breaking two well established school records in track. He is now the school’s all-time record holder in the 1600 and 3200 meters. He won the Double Crown this spring at the WACC Track Championship on May 5, setting new records of 9:24.12 in the 3200 meters, and 4:21.01 in the 1600 meters. articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco presents its newest exhibition, Still Lives in Contemporary Art, now through August 12. The exhibition brings together an international group of artists who have unique takes on contemporary art and still life. Each artist has created a work within a framework of Black diasporic identities and histories. The featured artists include Sadie Barnette, LaKela Brown, Elizabeth Colomba, Njideka Akunyili Crosby, David Antonio Cruz, Awol Erizku, Leslie Hewitt, Yashua Klos, Deana Lawson, Azikiwe Mohammed, Rashaad Newsome, Toyin Ojih Odutola, Paul Mpagi Sepuya, Devan Shimoyama, William Villalongo, and Brittney Leeanne Williams. To make a reservation, visit https://www. moadsf.org/exhibitions/elegies-still-lifes-in-contemporary-art. Devan Shimoyama’s Silk flowers canvas.

articles.text: Opening night of “Sculpture in the Garden” at Ruth Bancroft Gardens in Walnut Creek will take place on Friday, June 17 with an after-hours event beginning at 5:30 p.m. Now in its 28th year, the event is an annual art show and sale that combines sculptural art with the natural sculptural beauty of the Gardens. All sculptures are for sale. Admission to the event is free with regular garden admission. Featured artists include Ana Bianchi, Joe Bologna, Kevin Byall, Larry Colvin, Henriette Cons Ponte, Tam Doan, Jake Edwards, Douglas Heine, Roger Heitzman, Stan Huncilman, and Karina Kudymova. To purchase general admission tickets, visit https://www. ruthbancroftgarden.org/sculpture-show-2022/. The Ruth Bancroft Gardens and Nursery is famous for its extensive collection of succulents, cacti, California native plants, and other drought-tolerant plants. The garden was originally planted in 1972 by Ruth Bancroft when it was her private garden. It is now open six days a week for the education and enjoyment of the public. The Bancroft Gardens is located at 1552 Bancroft Road in Walnut Creek. Call (925) 944- 9352 for more information. Sculpture in the Garden is now in its 28th year.
articles.title: Ruth Bancroft Gardens celebrates 28th Year of Sculpture in the Garden

articles.text: San Francisco Opera will present Mozart’s Don Giovanni now through July 2. Don Giovanni, part three of the Mozart-Da Ponte Trilogy, is a dark comedy with a horrific twist ending. articles.text: It was a quiet afternoon in 2018 when Susan Freeman paused mid-sentence and asked, “Would you like to host some musicians for the Piedmont Chamber Music Festival?” The question wasn’t entirely from left field. We had recently hosted eight members of the Afghan Girls Robotics Team in our home. Susan had been a part of that, taking the girls one day to explore San Francisco. Knowing how much we had enjoyed that experience, Susan suggested our family might also want to host musicians for the weeklong music festival, especially since our son was a budding cellist. We had not known of the Piedmont Chamber Music Festival (PCMF), which was founded in 2016 by Wayne Lee, a Piedmont native, and his wife, Juliana Han. Susan had been involved from the beginning as the indefatigable box office manager. Her passion for the festival was contagious. Just hearing her talk about it, one would think that the PCMF was one of Piedmont’s best kept secrets. And she was right. So began our ties with the festival. The honor of hosting worldclass musicians in our home was an unforgettable experience. Not only did we get to enjoy their music, but we got to know the personalities and lives behind their music-making. And what could beat the privilege of attending concerts in the intimacy of Piedmont Center for the Arts without driving across the bridge to the festival’s early success. Friends of Susan would like to raise funds to sponsor Friday’s concert, July 22, in her memory. The program for this concert features A Sanguine Clockwork, composed by Paul Wiancko, a celebrated composer and cellist. He is also a past featured performer at the festival during the years that Susan was an active volunteer. In reference to A Sanguine Clockwork, Wiancko states, “The title of this work refers to the intricate inner workings of the human body as well as the joyful interconnectedness of human beings on a much larger scale. A Sanguine Clockwork explores the relationship between the molecular and the cultural – that inexplicable science which links the sentiment of a well-loved folk song to the blood in our veins.” On July 22, we hope to celebrate the “joyful interconnectedness” that Susan brought to all of us. If you would like to join us in sponsoring the concert in Susan’s honor, please visit piedmontcmf. org and click on Support. You may specify that your donation be applied to the concert honoring Susan Freeman. To volunteer for the festival or to host musicians, contact Susan Chamberlain at susanchacha@ gmail.com. Tickets for the Piedmont Chamber Music Festival are available at piedmontcmf.org. Concerts will be held July 20, 22, and 24. Following each concert is a reception and an opportunity to meet the musicians. Susan Freeman to Davies Symphony Hall? Parking, gas, and bridge toll combined were equivalent to the price of a PCMF ticket. Sadly, just two and a half years after introducing us to the festival, Susan passed away following a long but heroic battle with cancer. Susan’s mark can be found in so many facets of Piedmont. In fact, last year’s Turkey Trot was held in her memory, commemorating her 18 years of support. But perhaps Susan’s greatest legacy lies in the generations of youth who have benefited from her guidance in the college application process. For some students, she was as much life coach as counselor, helping them achieve not only success but, more importantly, happiness. For our family, she became a dear friend. From July 20-24 this summer the Piedmont Chamber Music Festival returns for its fifth season with the theme, “Human, Alone and Together.” It seems fitting to honor Susan’s contribution

pages.text: Wednesday, June 8, 2022 19 Piedmont Chamber Music Festival to honor Susan Freeman By Eliza and Doug Chin It was a quiet afternoon in 2018 when Susan Freeman paused mid-sentence and asked, “Would you like to host some musicians for the Piedmont Chamber Music Festival?” The question wasn’t entirely from left field. We had recently hosted eight members of the Afghan Girls Robotics Team in our home. Susan had been a part of that, taking the girls one day to explore San Francisco. Knowing how much we had enjoyed that experience, Susan suggested our family might also want to host musicians for the weeklong music festival, especially since our son was a budding cellist. We had not known of the Piedmont Chamber Music Festival (PCMF), which was founded in 2016 by Wayne Lee, a Piedmont native, and his wife, Juliana Han. Susan had been involved from the beginning as the indefatigable box office manager. Her passion for the festival was contagious. Just hearing her talk about it, one would think that the PCMF was one of Piedmont’s best kept secrets. And she was right. So began our ties with the festival. The honor of hosting worldclass musicians in our home was an unforgettable experience. Not only did we get to enjoy their music, but we got to know the personalities and lives behind their music-making. And what could beat the privilege of attending concerts in the intimacy of Piedmont Center for the Arts without driving across the bridge to the festival’s early success. Friends of Susan would like to raise funds to sponsor Friday’s concert, July 22, in her memory. The program for this concert features A Sanguine Clockwork, composed by Paul Wiancko, a celebrated composer and cellist. He is also a past featured performer at the festival during the years that Susan was an active volunteer. In reference to A Sanguine Clockwork, Wiancko states, “The title of this work refers to the intricate inner workings of the human body as well as the joyful interconnectedness of human beings on a much larger scale. A Sanguine Clockwork explores the relationship between the molecular and the cultural – that inexplicable science which links the sentiment of a well-loved folk song to the blood in our veins.” On July 22, we hope to celebrate the “joyful interconnectedness” that Susan brought to all of us. If you would like to join us in sponsoring the concert in Susan’s honor, please visit piedmontcmf. org and click on Support. You may specify that your donation be applied to the concert honoring Susan Freeman. To volunteer for the festival or to host musicians, contact Susan Chamberlain at susanchacha@ gmail.com. Tickets for the Piedmont Chamber Music Festival are available at piedmontcmf.org. Concerts will be held July 20, 22, and 24. Following each concert is a reception and an opportunity to meet the musicians. Saturday, June 11, 11 a.m. Opening of Diane Levy Art Exhibit Local artist Diane Levy founded the San Francisco Children’s Art Center at Fort Mason in San Francisco and taught art in West Oakland in a storefront studio. This exhibit, brought to us by her daughter Eve Haight, is an homage to her artwork, and honors her lifelong dedication to bringing art to children. Proceeds from all sales will go to Arts for Oakland Kids. Gallery hours are Saturday and Sunday, 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on the weekends of June 11-12 & 18-19, and Saturday, June 25. Saturday, June 11, 8 p.m. Susan Freeman to Davies Symphony Hall? Parking, gas, and bridge toll combined were equivalent to the price of a PCMF ticket. Sadly, just two and a half years after introducing us to the festival, Susan passed away following a long but heroic battle with cancer. Susan’s mark can be found in so many facets of Piedmont. In fact, last year’s Turkey Trot was held in her memory, commemorating her 18 years of support. But perhaps Susan’s greatest legacy lies in the generations of youth who have benefited from her guidance in the college application process. For some students, she was as much life coach as counselor, helping them achieve not only success but, more importantly, happiness. For our family, she became a dear friend. articles.text: A scene from Sofia Coppola’s film, The Beguiled. The Beguiled, released in 2017, opens with a young girl Amy (Oona Laurence), walking among the moss-covered trees of an aging southern estate. It’s 1864, one year before the end of the Civil War. The place is rural Virginia. She is humming to herself and in the distance is the hollow sound of cannon fire. Abruptly she comes upon a wounded union solder lying against a tree. His leg is bloodied and he can’t move. She agrees to help him back to the mansion of her all-girls’ school for southern belles, a place where they are waiting out the war, trying to carry on, though they know that the Union soldiers are slowly advancing. Amy, helping the soldier, corporal John McBurney (Colin Farrell), stops to ring a bell near a tall iron gate and then waits for help from head mistress, Martha Farnsworth (Nicole Kidman), and her charges, to include teacher Edwina Dabney (Kirsten Dunst). The presence of the corporal presents a dilemma. They can turn him over to the Confederate soldiers that often pass the school, or, as Mistress Farnsworth opines, they can do the Christian thing and clean and stitch his wound, give him time to heal, before turning him over to the Confederate army. They all agree that they should do the latter and it is that decision that changes in all ways, both subtle and obvious, the delicate balance of the school and its students. At first all is rigid decorum, the females in their high neck dresses, sitting down to their dinners served on fine china, candlelight giving a soft glow, their manners polite. During the day they labor in the garden. But gradually, like moths to a flame, the young women are pulled to McBurney’s room where he lies waiting to mend. As he meets each one, he is struck by his good fortune, his lyrical Irish brogue complementing each with a deft touch of kind words and seemingly sincere interest. Gradually the school environment, at first cool and suspicious of this enemy soldier, turns into a Southern hothouse of obsession and irresistible lust, expressed initially as a disguised formality but ultimately as something else entirely. What McBurney doesn’t realize is that it is not he who is spinning a web to ensnare the inhabitants of this seemingly benign school, but it is he who is the butterfly, pulled into their insulated, lonely world and caught, absent his awareness. While there is a war being fought over slavery just beyond the compound, and all of the slaves that once resided on the Farnsworth plantation have left, this film is not about the issues that perpetuated the war. Rather it is a study of characters, each one of them interpreting McBurney’s presence in her own way. That is the essence of what co-writer and director Sofia Coppola chose to make, one she manages very nicely with a superb ensemble. The Beguiled, Starring Colin Farrell, Nicole Kidman and Kirsten Dunst. Directed by Sofia Coppola. 1 hr., 53 min. Rated R. Released in 2017. articles.text: Kate Maberly, Andrew Knott and Heydon Prowse in The Secret Garden. The Secret Garden, released in 1993, is a family-friendly film. Adapted from the classic book of the same name, and written by Frances Hodgson Burnett in 1911. For more than a century it has been embraced by generations of young readers. As a movie, it is a visual delight, created by the same filmmakers responsible for the equally extraordinary Black Stallion. The story focuses on 10-yearold Mary Lennox (Kate Maberly), an unsmiling British girl, orphaned while living in India. Tragically, her parents died in an earthquake, and she is sent to live with her uncle, Lord Craven (John Lynch), at his bleak manor called Misselthwaite. A widower, heartbroken, he has spent a decade reclusively mourning the death of his wife. Upon her arrival, Mary realizes that she will be looked after by the manor’s strict and unsympathetic housekeeper, Mrs. Medlock (Maggie Smith). Mary is taken to her room and admonished not to wander about. Of course, curious, she discovers countless narrow passageways and musty rooms, the sparse furniture covered with dusty sheets. To her surprise, she discovers a musty, dark room with its curtains closed inhabited by her 10-year-old cousin, Colin Craven (Heydon Prowse). The boy is Lord Craven’s bedridden son who is treated like a fragile invalid. He is short-tempered, indulged by the house staff, and ever demanding. He never leaves his room and believes that the world outside is filled with dangerous “spores.” Continuing her exploration of the manor and then its grounds, Mary discovers a long-neglected walled-in garden. Using a large key that she found in one of the rooms, she opens an ivy-covered door, only to find the trees and plants brittle and brown. By chance she also meets another boy, Dickon Sowerby (Andrew Knott), similar in age, who is the younger brother of one the housemaids, Martha (Laura Crossley). He is a free spirit and believes he can talk to animals. Together, they begin to restore the secret garden. At the same time Mary begins the process of convincing the recalcitrant Colin that he can indeed venture outside and be unharmed. Soon, along with Dickon, she takes him to see the hidden sanctuary where Colin, along with the garden, begins the magical journey of restoration. He is soon standing on unsteady legs and taking tentative steps. Of course, the garden is a metaphor. At the outset it is a symbol of sadness and loss. But as it changes – flowers bloom, the trees turn green, birds return – the stark sadness of the manor lifts. The three children, and Lord Craven as well, are transformed, which eventually leads to a heartwarming conclusion. The Secret Garden. Directed by Agnieszka Holland. Starring Kate Maberly, Heydon Prowse, and Maggie Smith. 1 hr., 41 min. Rated G. Released in 1993. Now streaming on HBO/VUDU/Apple TV.

articles.text: Kelly Reno stars in The Black Stallion. The Black Stallion, released in 1979, and adapted from the classic 1941 children’s book written by Walter Farley, is a breathtakingly beautiful film, timeless and filled with innocent wonder. The story begins somewhere off the coast of Africa. Pre-teen Alec Ramsey (Kelly Reno) and his father (Hoyt Axon) are travelling north on a steamer. It is the summer of 1946. As Alec boards the ship, he pauses to watch a group of men trying to subdue a magnificent black Arabian stallion and get it into a stable. Later that night, Alec, sound asleep, is thrown out of his bunk by an explosion, caused by a fire in the engine room. The ship is sinking. Alec’s first thought is of the horse and he runs topside and frees the stallion, which jumps over the railing into the ocean. Alec is swept overboard by a crashing wave. Later, in the early morning, he finds himself lying on a sandy beach. Uncertain where he is, still dressed in his pajamas, he begins to explore what proves to be a deserted island. To his surprise, he encounters the black horse, its harness snagged in the rocks. Using a pocketknife given to him by his father the evening before the fire, he manages to cut the horse free and the stallion races off. Using the knife, Alec learns to fish and finds that seaweed is edible. He often spots the stallion, which he names “The Black,” running along the beach. Gathering some seaweed in a large frond, he places it at the water’s edge and waits. Curious and hungry, the horse tentatively approaches the seaweed. Before long The Black is eating from Alec’s hand, and so the two fashion a bond. Soon Alec is riding the stallion across the stretching sand, creating a kind of poetry as the boy and horse become one. Weeks pass, and unexpectedly a fishing boat anchors just off shore and Alec and the horse are both rescued. Together they return to America and to the boy’s mother (Teri Garr), now widowed. The Black is kept in their fenced-in back yard; however, it soon escapes through an open gate and gallops through town. Alec, desperate to find the horse, finally finds him in an old barn owned by Henry Dailey (Mickey Rooney). And so act three begins. Alec discovers that Henry was once a jockey and trainer. Henry soon comes to realize how extraordinary The Black is, having remarkable speed. The idea comes to Henry to enter the stallion in a much publicized match race, and so they begin to prepare, Henry teaching Alec to ride like a jockey while exercising The Black on an oval racetrack. Of course, the story is familiar, reminding us of the classic film National Velvet, also starring Mickey Rooney. Naturally, The Black Stallion will have an exciting conclusion, and kids of all ages will be captivated by what proves to be wonderful fable. The Black Stallion. Directed by Carroll Ballard. Starring Kelly Reno, Mickey Rooney, and Teri Garr. 1 hr., 58 min. Rated G. Released in 1979. Now screening on VUDU/Netflix/Prime.

articles.text: One of my favorite things to do when on vacation in France is to visit the local charcuterie shop. I am always amazed by the wonderful variety of products available, many of which are unknown in the U.S. There will often be 10 types of pate, goose, duck and pork rilliettes, tons of different types of salami, confit of goose and duck, foie gras of various sorts – an amazing panoply of meaty goodness. Over the years of travel to France, I realized you do not even have to find a charcuterie shop to locate these products. Any good French Supermarche, like Leclerc, Casino, Intermarche, or Carrefour, will have a long charcuterie counter where you can purchase the same quality of products that you find in the small shops. After years of smuggling home pate and rillettes in my suitcase, I was amazed and delighted to discover the wonderful Fabrique Delices here in he East Bay. It was a dream come true – a company started by French entrepreneurs to create French-style charcuterie in America. On top of that it was nearby in Hayward. The company began in 1920 in Meaux, France and was called SAPAR. It became the leading producer of pates in Europe, with its products carried by Fauchon in Paris as well as gourmet stores all over Europe. In 1985 Jean Claude Auge decided to establish Fabrique Delices and bring French charcuterie to the American market. The idea was to produce products of outstanding and consistent quality with unique and eye-catching presentations. In 1996 Marc Poinsignon and Antonio Pinheiro were brought from France to oversee the U.S. subsidiary. In 2002 Fabrique Delices moved into a newly built plant in Hayward, and today it is the largest producer of French charcuterie in America. I reached out to Fabrique Delices president Sebastien EspiDuck Rilletes nasse about the idea of throwing a dinner party to highlight some of their products. He loved the idea, so I recruited my Kensington Road neighbors Mike, Drennen, Jennifer, Jason, Megan, Ittai, and Margaret to be my guinea pigs. We started with the duck and pork rillettes. Most Americans know about pate, but not many know rillettes which are very popular in France. Every charcuterie place has big bowls of duck, goose and pork rillettes which they scoop out for you. It is basically moist meat mixed with extra fat which gives it an incredibly rich taste. You spread it on crusty French bread and finish with a tart cornichon pickle to cut the fat. Both types of rillettes were good, but the nod went to the duck. There was something almost decadent about spreading this essence of duck on bread. We progressed to the salumi course, which featured Dry Coppa, Wild Boar Salami and Black Truffle Salami. The Coppa was a large 6-inch diameter log of fat marbled meat similar to what you might find in an Italian deli. It was tasty and well received but I found its girth made it difficult to slice thin enough with just a knife. The Wild Boar salami was very intense and dark. The label said it was made from feral pigs (where do you get those?) and it did have a sort of “wild” taste. It was really great, especially with a piece of Conte cheese and some bread, but by far the favorite salami was the Black truffle. Considering how expensive they are, I did not expect it to really have that much truffle flavor. But was I wrong. This salami Fabrique Delices in Hayward offers 10 types of pate, goose, duck and pork rilliettes, different types of salami, confit of goose and duck, and foie gras of various sorts.

articles.text: Jim Wulfsberg, a longtime former Piedmont resident with a larger-than-life personality and a wide circle of friends, passed away on May 28, 2022 from metastatic ocular melanoma. He died peacefully in his home in Reno, Nevada surrounded by his dear wife and loving family. He was 78. Born Harold James Wulfsberg on May 24, 1944 in Long Beach, California, he was the son of Rudolf Einer Wulfsberg and Margaret Grace Adams Wulfsberg. He graduated from Woodrow Wilson High School as a football star and thespian, often commanding shared lead roles with his twin brother, Richard. Jim graduated from high school with highest honors and went on to graduate Summa Cum Laude from the University of Southern California. He completed his law degree at the University of California Berkeley at Boalt Hall School of Law in 1969. He was chairman at Wulfsberg, Reese & Colvig, where he practiced construction law representing a diverse clientele worldwide. Jim was known as a powerhouse litigator, often being referred to as a force of nature in the courtroom. Among his many talents, Jim was an outstanding athlete, competing in multiple marathons and triathlons over his illustrious career. At age 55, he won the Vine Man Ironman in his age group. Jim continued with his passion for running and cycling in beautiful locations around the world from Lake Tahoe to Tuscany. Spending quality time with his beautiful wife, Janet, his loving family, and dear friends was paramount to Jim. He squeezed every ounce of joy out of life and was a shining example of living Jim Wulfsberg life to the fullest. Jim is survived by his wife Janet, daughter Analisa, oldest son, Tyler and his wife Brittany, and his youngest son Todd and his wife Dianne. He is also survived by his brothers Richard and David Wulfsberg, sister Elaine Hutchinson, and by grandchildren Schuyler, Safira, Isabella, Addisyn, Ellison, Hannah, Lindyn and Alannah. Jim touched so many people all over the world but he made the greatest impact on the family that he leaves behind. In lieu of flowers, the family suggests making a memorial donation to any of the following charitable organizations: • The Navy SEAL Foundation: https://www.navysealfoundation.org • Tunnel to Towers Foundation: https://www.t2t.org • The Wounded Warrior Project: https://www.woundedwarriorproject.org The family will announce a memorial service at a later date.

articles.text: According to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), an individual’s carbon footprint is the aggregate of activities — such as using electricity, driving a car, or disposing of waste — that cause greenhouse gas emissions. The EPA’s Carbon Footprint Calculator (https://www3.epa.gov/ carbon-footprint-calculator/) estimates your footprint in three areas: home energy, transportation, and waste, according to your location, habits, and personal choices. The calculator estimates greenhouse gas emissions, including carbon dioxide – the gas most commonly emitted by humans – and methane, nitrous oxide, and fluorinated gases. These gases are known to trap heat in the atmosphere and cause climate change, or what is also known as global warming. Much of our individual carbon footprint is the result of our consumption, commonly defined as the items which we purchase with the largest contributors including food, clothing, and other household items. In relation to food, summer means that many tasty fruits and vegetables are in season and available locally. Shopping for food that has been produced and grown within a closer geographic region can reduce “food miles” and as a result its carbon footprint. Another piece to consider is food waste, both at the grocery store and in your own home. When disposing of your food waste, you can reduce methane emissions by diverting food waste to a composting facility rather than a landfill. Finally, it’s important to stay hydrated this summer! Think twice about buying plastic water bottles and use a reusable water bottle instead. Another significant portion of an individual carbon footprint is emissions from both day-to-day and holiday travel. Opting for a stay-at-home vacation, or one that doesn’t require flying, can significantly reduce your personal or family carbon footprint. Emissions from domestic aviation alone have increased 17% since 1990, to account for 9% of greenhouse gas emissions from the U.S. transportation sector. Flights departing from airports in the United States and its territories are responsible for almost one-quarter of global passenger transport-related carbon emissions. Using shared or active transportation, like busses, trains, and bikes, can reduce the emitted greenhouse gas emissions from personal travel by more than one half. Plus, active transportation like biking and walking can be a fun summer activity to help you and your family get out of the house! Finally, energy and natural gas used within your home on a daily basis consist of one of the largest factors in calculating your individual carbon footprint. Replacing your HVAC and water heating systems with heat pump technology can result in at least three to four times more energy savings than gas appliances. While some local incentives, such as the TECH Clean California program, are currently exhausted of funding, other local programs can help electrify your home and reduce the amount of energy your home is using. Through the Bay Area Regional Energy Network (BayREN) Home+ Program, single-family homeowners are eligible for a wide range of incentives, from Heat Pump Water Heaters to Heat Pump HVAC systems, in addition to insulation, duct sealing or replacement, and more. Further, The Rising Sun Center for Opportunity provides energy and water efficiency services, called Green House Calls, to households throughout the Bay Area. When you sign up for a Green House Call, an energy and water efficiency kit will be mailed to your door. Finally, the Electrify Everything in Your Home guide is a free resource that includes information about options for electric appliances, how to get started, questions to ask contractors, suggestions for how to best run appliances, and links to more information. Find electrification planning materials on the Rewiring America website. Annie Wensley is Piedmont’s Climate Action Fellow. She can be reached at awensley@piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: When I tell people the tale that as a Piedmont boy at age 12 in 1966, I possessed a young lad’s summer dream car in a stripped down shell of a red 1960 Vespa 400-they do not believe me. When I relive the events related to this magic car, they bring smiles and laughter 56 years later. Without this Polaroid photo, no one would ever believe the trouble we got into and the havoc caused when riding around Piedmont in this bare motorless mini, micro car. How does a young boy acquire such a rare vehicle and become envied by all the other young dreamers? Simple, you wander over to Nace Avenue, where you bump into your 18-year-old family friend who had blown the engine on his Vespa 400. He had just finished stripping the Vespa down to 4 wheels, brakes, emergency brake and steering. No doors, hoods, transmission, engine, glass, etc. With all of the parts removed, it weighed only about 350 pounds. So I asked Lowell if I could have the car, and he said yes. I just drove off on a cloud. The light weight of the car meant that three or four young 12-year-olds could easily push it all over town, in exchange for riding in it if you were lucky, – or maybe even driving it. We drove it over to Linda Beach playground and would take turns driving it down the asphalt pathway to the lower playground with several of us on it. We left with only minor mishaps. The next stop would be Piedmont Park and at the stores, now Wells Fargo Bank. Then it was onto Magnolia Avenue, where all of us took turns driving down the hill. What did the Police think about all of this? We talked with them, and since the car had no motor it fell into a gray area regarding possible citations. They requested only that we keep it on the sidewalk. We had the whole summer on our hands and could be seen in Mountain View Cemetery, and down by Lake Merritt. He died peacefully in his home in Reno, Nevada surrounded by his dear wife and loving family. He was 78. Born Harold James Wulfsberg on May 24, 1944 in Long Beach, California, he was the son of Rudolf Einer Wulfsberg and Margaret Grace Adams Wulfsberg. He graduated from Woodrow Wilson High School as a football star and thespian, often commanding shared lead roles with his twin brother, Richard. Jim graduated from high school with highest honors and went on to graduate Summa Cum Laude from the University of Southern California. He completed his law degree at the University of California Berkeley at Boalt Hall School of Law in 1969. He was chairman at Wulfsberg, Reese & Colvig, where he practiced construction law representing a diverse clientele worldwide. Jim was known as a powerhouse litigator, often being referred to as a force of nature in the courtroom. Among his many talents, Jim was an outstanding athlete, competing in multiple marathons and triathlons over his illustrious career. At age 55, he won the Vine Man Ironman in his age group. Jim continued with his passion for running and cycling in beautiful locations around the world from Lake Tahoe to Tuscany. Spending quality time with his beautiful wife, Janet, his loving family, and dear friends was paramount to Jim. He squeezed every ounce of joy out of life and was a shining example of living Jim Wulfsberg life to the fullest. Jim is survived by his wife Janet, daughter Analisa, oldest son, Tyler and his wife Brittany, and his youngest son Todd and his wife Dianne. He is also survived by his brothers Richard and David Wulfsberg, sister Elaine Hutchinson, and by grandchildren Schuyler, Safira, Isabella, Addisyn, Ellison, Hannah, Lindyn and Alannah. READ IT IN THE POST By Annie Wensley According to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), an individual’s carbon footprint is the aggregate of activities — such as using electricity, driving a car, or disposing of waste — that cause greenhouse gas emissions. The EPA’s Carbon Footprint Calculator (https://www3.epa.gov/ carbon-footprint-calculator/) estimates your footprint in three areas: home energy, transportation, and waste, according to your location, habits, and personal choices. The calculator estimates greenhouse gas emissions, including carbon dioxide – the gas most commonly emitted by humans – and methane, nitrous oxide, and fluorinated gases. These gases are known to trap heat in the atmosphere and cause climate change, or what is also known as global warming. Much of our individual carbon footprint is the result of our consumption, commonly defined as the items which we purchase with the largest contributors including food, clothing, and other household items. In relation to food, summer means that many tasty fruits and vegetables are in season and available locally. Shopping for food that has been produced and grown within a closer geographic region can reduce “food miles” and as a result its carbon footprint. Another piece to consider is food waste, both at the grocery How to reduce your carbon footprint this summer store and in your own home. When disposing of your food waste, you can reduce methane emissions by diverting food waste to a composting facility rather than a landfill. Finally, it’s important to stay hydrated this summer! Think twice about buying plastic water bottles and use a reusable water bottle instead. Another significant portion of an individual carbon footprint is emissions from both day-to-day and holiday travel. Opting for a stay-at-home vacation, or one that doesn’t require flying, can significantly reduce your personal or family carbon footprint. Emissions from domestic aviation alone have increased 17% since 1990, to account for 9% of greenhouse gas emissions from the U.S. transportation sector. Flights departing from airports in the United States and its territories are responsible for almost one-quarter of global passenger transport-related carbon emissions. Using shared or active transportation, like busses, trains, and bikes, can reduce the emitted greenhouse gas emissions from personal travel by more than one half. Plus, active transportation like biking and walking can be a fun summer activity to help you and your family get out of the house! Finally, energy and natural gas used within your home on a daily basis consist of one of the largest factors in calculating your individual carbon footprint. Replacing your HVAC and water heating systems with heat pump technology can result in at least three to four times more energy savings than gas appliances. While some local incentives, such as the TECH Clean California program, are currently exhausted of funding, other local programs can help electrify your home and reduce the amount of energy your home is using. Through the Bay Area Regional Energy Network (BayREN) Home+ Program, single-family homeowners are eligible for a wide range of incentives, from Heat Pump Water Heaters to Heat Pump HVAC systems, in addition to insulation, duct sealing or replacement, and more. Further, The Rising Sun Center for Opportunity provides energy and water efficiency services, called Green House Calls, to households throughout the Bay Area. When you sign up for a Green House Call, an energy and water efficiency kit will be mailed to your door. Finally, the Electrify Everything in Your Home guide is a free resource that includes information about options for electric appliances, how to get started, questions to ask contractors, suggestions for how to best run appliances, and links to more information. Find electrification planning materials on the Rewiring America website. Annie Wensley is Piedmont’s Climate Action Fellow. She can be reached at awensley@piedmont.ca.gov. If photos could speak – the Summer of 1966 By Neil Teixeira When I tell people the tale that as a Piedmont boy at age 12 in 1966, I possessed a young lad’s summer dream car in a stripped down shell of a red 1960 Vespa 400-they do not believe me. When I relive the events related to this magic car, they bring smiles and laughter 56 years later. Without this Polaroid photo, no one would ever believe the trouble we got into and the havoc caused when riding around Piedmont in this bare motorless mini, micro car. How does a young boy acquire such a rare vehicle and become envied by all the other young dreamers? Simple, you wander over to Nace Avenue, where you bump into your 18-year-old family friend who had blown the engine on his Vespa 400. He had just finished stripping the Vespa down to 4 wheels, brakes, emergency brake and steering. No doors, hoods, transmission, engine, glass, etc. With all of the parts removed, it weighed only about 350 pounds. So I asked Lowell if I could have the car, and he said yes. I just drove off on a cloud. The light weight of the car meant that three or four young 12-year-olds could easily push it all over town, in exchange for riding in it if you were lucky, – or maybe even driving it. We drove it over to Linda Beach playground and would take turns driving it down the asphalt pathway to the lower playground with several of us on it. We left with only minor mishaps. The next stop would be Piedmont Park and at the stores, now Wells Fargo Bank. Then it was onto Magnolia Avenue, where all of us took turns driving down the hill. What did the Police think about all of this? We talked with them, and since the car had no motor it fell into a gray area regarding possible citations. They requested only that we keep it on the sidewalk. We had the whole summer on our hands and could be seen in Mountain View Cemetery, and down by Lake Merritt. We would get up early in the morning with everyone waiting outside for the day’s adventure. Everywhere we went, other young groups pleaded for a ride or to drive it. People wanted to trade for it or buy it from us. We all have very fond memories of our Summer of 1966 and the one-of-a-kind Vespa 400. For a few short weeks we had magic on four wheels. During the previous Wednesday walk, the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group took their second of Will Adams’ tour of Albert Farr-designed Piedmont homes, ending at the home of Dave and Nancy DeRoche where Farr once lived. The DeRoches welcomed the walkers for a visit and refreshments. Nancy also offered to take the group on a later tour of their upper Oakland Avenue neighborhood, which continues up to Blair and Scenic Avenues. The group happily accepted Nancy’s offer for their next walk, but they didn’t know what an additional treat it would be. The weather on June 1 was more than cooperating – a beautiful, warm Piedmont morning. There was a strong turnout of 35 walkers and one K-9. Before the tour It was announced that Phil Witte, a regular walker and a cartoonist with the Post, is having an exhibit of his cartoons at Dominican University in San Rafael opening June 18. Nancy announced that her tour would take the group past the Sutro mansion on Blair Avenue, She also announced that there is a tour of the gardens at the Shartsis home on Sunday, June 12. (More information is available at https://www.gardenconservancy.org/open-days/garden-directory/the-shartsis-gardens.) The area above Oakland Avenue was a bit of Bohemian neighborhood in the early 20th Century. Writers and painters including Jack London and Xavier Martinez lived there in some unique homes. Before them, Frank C. Havens and his nephew George Sterling were also important residents. Nancy led the walkers a house that might have been an early office for Havens, a real estate developer in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. He partnered with Francis “Borax” Smith, a businessman who made his fortune in borax mining but also invested in real estate. He and Havens created the Realty Syndicate in 1895, which developed many of Oakland and Piedmont’s neighborhoods. The group continued uphill on on Blair Avenue where Nancy pointed out the top of a home hidden by other homes. She said it is the Sutro mansion (the Shartsis residence). The Sutro mansion with five gardens is behind it further up the hill, but is barely visible. Earler a much smaller, craftsman-style home was built there in 1876-77 by Joseph Worcester. This house has a special claim to fame. It was there that Jack London lived and wrote his classic novel, The Call of the Wild in 1902-03. The house has a cedar shake shingle exterior, and was enlarged after it was moved by adding a new first floor. London was a prominent part of the artist colony that occupied this part of Piedmont in the early 1900s. He was a free-spirited man who sailed to the Orient, drank freely, and had at least three important women in his life. The success of The Call of the Wild provided him with considerable wealth, and he built a separate home for first wife, Bessie, and two daughters, Joan and Becky, further up the hill on Scenic Avenue. He was building his own grand home in Glen Ellen, but it burned to the ground shortly before it was completed. Sadly, London died at age 40 from the continuing effects of a tropical disease that he contracted during his travels and his drinking. The group made their way down this narrow part of Scenic, and made their way home on Piedmont’s longest pedestrian pathway, the 281 stairs that connect Blair and Scenic. The group thanked Nancy for providing a wonderful tour of her historic neighborhood. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.n. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. For others, being home has only highlighted what we don’t like about our property. If you’re looking to improve your living spaces, increase the value of your home to sell in the future at a higher value, here are some ideas to help you do just that with minimal effort. Utilizing spaces that are otherwise not used is a great place to start. Do you have a closet in your home collecting junk? Take that footage and connect it to an adjacent room to increase the living space. If the layout of your home isn’t serving your needs, combine two underutilized rooms into a grand larger room with more appeal. A qualified contractor can determine which walls are load-bearing and help you explore your options to create a more open living space. If you aren’t prepared to do a major remodel, minor changes can have a big impact on the aesthetics of your home. Using wallpaper or fresh, updated colors on walls, replacing countertops or tile, and refinishing rather than replacing cabinetry make big changes to your home without the expense of a major remodel. Wallpaper and matching wall switches creates glamour in a powder room. Recessed lighting and fresh paint update a classic room. Updating your lighting, by replacing ceiling and wall fixtures or installing recessed lighting, will have a powerful impact on your environment. Today’s lighting is more energy efficient, so you’ll also see the benefit on your monthly utility bill. Don’t forget the exterior of your home. Replacing your garage door with a more modern design can greatly increase the curb appeal of your home. Decking or a new patio will add extra living space as well as an interesting look and design to your property. Repairing cracks in your driveway, adding gravel to pathways and updating your landscaping complete the look. articles.text: On the last day of school, Thursday, June 2, Park View Avenue was closed off for a block party for kids in the neighborhood. A fifteen foot inflatable waterslide inhabited the street and kids quickly embraced the summer spirit. The block that runs below the PHS baseball Field and Wildwood’s lower playground epitomizes the Piedmont spirit. Even in the thick of the pandemic, in July of 2020, the block came together for the house decorating Fourth of July competition and won the Highland Spoon for “Best Quaranteam.” On Thursday, tables were set out in the street for food, and the Yeh family provided a slushie machine operated by daughter Coral Yeh and her friend MacKenzie Seto-Nguyen. With the street blocked off and reserved for fun, kids rode their bikes, scooters and big wheels. Even Piedmont Police Juvenile Officer Hugo Diaz stopped by to say hello and hand out water balloons. Within hours of school letting out, students traded their backpacks and pencils for swim trunks and water guns. The special occasion was a welcome sight after 2-1/2 years of restrictions due to COVID-19. Kids celebrated making it through another year and the anticipation of what everyone hopes will be life back to normal this summer. A giant inflatable water slide pumped up the start of summer spirit on Park View Avenue. Coral Yeh (left) and MacKenzie Seto-Nguyen served slushies to the revelers at the block party. Park View Avenue hosted a day of fun for kids on the block Thursday, June 2 in the afternoon prior to high school graduation at nearby Witter Field. Juvenile Officer Hugo Diaz stopped by to offer some water balloons. He is pictured with Annabelle Malione enjoying a slushie. Deer spotted in yard on lower piedmont.
